elements.name: Whole-Part
elements.what: An aggregate component (the Whole) encapsulates constituent Part objects, organizes their collaboration, and is the sole access point to their combined functionality.
elements.problem: Clients need to treat an assembly of cooperating objects as a single semantic unit without depending on, or bypassing, its internal parts.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 1: A System of Patterns - Buschmann, Meunier, Rohnert, Sommerlad, Stal (1996)

elements.name: Master-Slave
elements.what: A master component partitions work into semantically identical sub-tasks, delegates them to interchangeable slave components, and combines their results into the final answer.
elements.problem: Divide-and-conquer for fault tolerance, parallel speed-up, or computational accuracy, while keeping clients unaware that the service is internally replicated or partitioned.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 1: A System of Patterns - Buschmann, Meunier, Rohnert, Sommerlad, Stal (1996)

elements.name: Proxy
elements.what: A placeholder object with the same interface as a subject controls access to it, adding indirection for lazy loading, protection, remoting, caching, or bookkeeping.
elements.problem: Clients should not need direct access to an object that is expensive, remote, protected, or requires added housekeeping on each access.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software - Gamma, Helm, Johnson, Vlissides (1994)

elements.name: Command Processor
elements.what: A dedicated processor component manages user requests reified as command objects: it schedules, executes, logs, and stores them, enabling undo/redo and macro services.
elements.problem: Applications need flexible, decoupled handling of requests plus request-level services (undo, logging, scheduling, macros) that the request initiators should not implement themselves.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 1: A System of Patterns - Buschmann, Meunier, Rohnert, Sommerlad, Stal (1996)

elements.name: View Handler
elements.what: A view handler component manages all views of an application: it opens, coordinates, tiles, clones, updates, and closes them through a uniform view interface.
elements.problem: Multi-view applications need centralized, extensible management of view lifecycle and inter-view coordination instead of scattering it across the views.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 1: A System of Patterns - Buschmann, Meunier, Rohnert, Sommerlad, Stal (1996)

elements.name: Forwarder-Receiver
elements.what: Peers communicate through paired forwarder and receiver intermediaries that encapsulate marshaling, delivery mechanism, and endpoint mapping behind a simple send/receive interface.
elements.problem: Peer components need transparent inter-process communication without hard-coding the IPC mechanism, so the transport can be exchanged without touching peer logic.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 1: A System of Patterns - Buschmann, Meunier, Rohnert, Sommerlad, Stal (1996)

elements.name: Client-Dispatcher-Server
elements.what: A dispatcher component sits between clients and servers, providing name-to-server resolution and connection establishment so clients request services by name only.
elements.problem: Clients should stay independent of server location and connection details; a level of indirection provides location transparency and late binding of services.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 1: A System of Patterns - Buschmann, Meunier, Rohnert, Sommerlad, Stal (1996)
elements.borderline: Distribution-flavored, but implementable as an in-process dispatcher/registry inside one program; POSA1 classes it as a design pattern.

elements.name: Publisher-Subscriber
elements.what: Publishers notify dynamically registered subscribers of state changes or events through a subscription interface, keeping both sides maximally decoupled.
elements.problem: One-to-many change propagation where the set of interested components varies at runtime and publishers must not depend on concrete consumers; POSA1's event-channel variant generalizes GoF Observer.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 1: A System of Patterns - Buschmann, Meunier, Rohnert, Sommerlad, Stal (1996)

elements.name: Counted Pointer
elements.what: A handle class embeds a reference counter in (or beside) a dynamically allocated body object, updating it on copy/assignment/destruction and deleting the body when the count reaches zero.
elements.problem: Shared dynamically allocated objects in C++ need deterministic deallocation without ownership ambiguity, dangling pointers, or leaks.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 1: A System of Patterns - Buschmann, Meunier, Rohnert, Sommerlad, Stal (1996)

elements.name: Wrapper Facade
elements.what: Concise, cohesive, type-safe class interfaces encapsulate low-level, non-portable system APIs (sockets, threads, mutexes) and their associated data.
elements.problem: Programming directly against low-level C-style OS APIs is verbose, error-prone, and non-portable; wrapping them yields robustness and portability without significant overhead.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 2: Patterns for Concurrent and Networked Objects - Schmidt, Stal, Rohnert, Buschmann (2000)

elements.name: Component Configurator
elements.what: An application links and unlinks component implementations at runtime via a uniform component lifecycle interface (init, suspend, resume, fini) and a central configurator, without recompiling or restarting.
elements.problem: Which component implementations run, and when, should be decided late (deployment/runtime) and be changeable dynamically, decoupling implementation from configuration time.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 2: Patterns for Concurrent and Networked Objects - Schmidt, Stal, Rohnert, Buschmann (2000)

elements.name: Interceptor
elements.what: A framework exposes dispatch points where registered interceptor objects are invoked automatically on framework-internal events, letting services be added transparently via callbacks and context objects.
elements.problem: Frameworks must be extensible with out-of-band services (logging, security, monitoring) after deployment without changing framework or application code.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 2: Patterns for Concurrent and Networked Objects - Schmidt, Stal, Rohnert, Buschmann (2000)

elements.name: Extension Interface
elements.what: A component exports multiple role-specific interfaces reachable through a root interface (QueryInterface-style), rather than one ever-growing interface.
elements.problem: Prevents interface bloat and client breakage when components evolve new capabilities; clients depend only on the interface roles they use.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 2: Patterns for Concurrent and Networked Objects - Schmidt, Stal, Rohnert, Buschmann (2000)

elements.name: Reactor
elements.what: A synchronous event demultiplexer (select/poll) waits on multiple event sources and dispatches ready events to registered handler objects, serially, in one thread of control.
elements.problem: A server must service many clients or I/O sources concurrently without one thread per connection, while keeping application-level event handling single-threaded and simple.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 2: Patterns for Concurrent and Networked Objects - Schmidt, Stal, Rohnert, Buschmann (2000)

elements.name: Proactor
elements.what: Applications initiate asynchronous operations and a completion dispatcher later invokes the matching completion handlers when the OS finishes the operations.
elements.problem: Exploit OS-level asynchronous I/O for throughput while structuring the resulting completion-driven control flow so application code stays modular and mechanism-independent.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 2: Patterns for Concurrent and Networked Objects - Schmidt, Stal, Rohnert, Buschmann (2000)

elements.name: Asynchronous Completion Token
elements.what: The initiator of an asynchronous operation passes along an opaque token that comes back with the completion event, letting the response be demultiplexed to the right state and actions in constant time.
elements.problem: When responses to async operations arrive out of order, the receiver must efficiently re-associate each completion with the context needed to process it, without searching.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 2: Patterns for Concurrent and Networked Objects - Schmidt, Stal, Rohnert, Buschmann (2000)

elements.name: Acceptor-Connector
elements.what: Connection establishment and service initialization (acceptor for passive, connector for active roles) are decoupled from the service processing performed once a connection is established.
elements.problem: Connection setup logic changes independently of application service logic; separating them enables reuse of either and supports both synchronous and asynchronous establishment.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 2: Patterns for Concurrent and Networked Objects - Schmidt, Stal, Rohnert, Buschmann (2000)

elements.name: Scoped Locking
elements.what: A guard object acquires a lock in its constructor and releases it in its destructor, so every exit path from a scope (including exceptions) releases the lock.
elements.problem: Manually paired lock/unlock calls leak locks on early returns and exceptions; RAII applied to locks makes release automatic and exception-safe.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 2: Patterns for Concurrent and Networked Objects - Schmidt, Stal, Rohnert, Buschmann (2000)

elements.name: Strategized Locking
elements.what: The synchronization mechanism a component uses is a pluggable strategy (template parameter or polymorphic lock object), including a null lock for single-threaded configurations.
elements.problem: The same component must run efficiently under different concurrency models; hard-wiring one lock type either wastes performance or sacrifices safety.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 2: Patterns for Concurrent and Networked Objects - Schmidt, Stal, Rohnert, Buschmann (2000)

elements.name: Thread-Safe Interface
elements.what: Public interface methods acquire the component's lock and then delegate to non-locking private implementation methods; implementation methods never call locking interface methods.
elements.problem: Intra-component method calls under a non-recursive mutex cause self-deadlock or needless locking overhead; a locking discipline at the interface boundary avoids both.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 2: Patterns for Concurrent and Networked Objects - Schmidt, Stal, Rohnert, Buschmann (2000)

elements.name: Double-Checked Locking
elements.what: Code checks a condition (typically 'initialized?') before and again after acquiring a lock, so the common already-initialized path skips locking entirely.
elements.problem: Thread-safe lazy initialization of shared state without paying lock overhead on every access; note the pattern is broken without memory-ordering guarantees (fences/atomics), a hazard documented since its publication.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 2: Patterns for Concurrent and Networked Objects - Schmidt, Stal, Rohnert, Buschmann (2000)

elements.name: Thread-Specific Storage
elements.what: Each thread gets its own copy of a logically global datum, accessed through one 'global' access point that transparently resolves to the calling thread's instance.
elements.problem: Data such as errno or per-thread caches must be globally reachable yet not shared, avoiding both lock contention and explicit parameter threading.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 2: Patterns for Concurrent and Networked Objects - Schmidt, Stal, Rohnert, Buschmann (2000)

elements.name: Active Object
elements.what: Method invocation is decoupled from method execution: calls are reified as requests on an activation queue and executed by the object's own thread via a scheduler, with futures for results.
elements.problem: An object needs its own thread of control so clients are not blocked and its internal state is accessed by one thread only, serializing concurrency at the object boundary.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 2: Patterns for Concurrent and Networked Objects - Schmidt, Stal, Rohnert, Buschmann (2000)

elements.name: Monitor Object
elements.what: An object synchronizes its own method execution with an internal lock plus condition variables, so at most one method runs at a time and methods can wait for state conditions inside the object.
elements.problem: Multiple threads share one object; the object itself, not its clients, should enforce mutual exclusion and cooperative scheduling on its state (mechanism rooted in Hoare's 1974 monitors).
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 2: Patterns for Concurrent and Networked Objects - Schmidt, Stal, Rohnert, Buschmann (2000)

elements.name: Half-Sync/Half-Async
elements.what: Concurrent processing is split into an asynchronous layer (interrupt/event-driven) and a synchronous layer (blocking service threads) mediated by a queueing layer between them.
elements.problem: Combine the performance of asynchronous event handling with the programming simplicity of synchronous code, without either style polluting the other.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 2: Patterns for Concurrent and Networked Objects - Schmidt, Stal, Rohnert, Buschmann (2000)
elements.borderline: POSA2 labels it architectural, but it is a within-process/within-subsystem layering (e.g. OS network stacks, single servers), so it passes the altitude test.

elements.name: Leader/Followers
elements.what: A pool of threads takes turns: one leader waits for and demultiplexes an event, promotes a follower to be the new leader, then processes the event itself before rejoining the followers.
elements.problem: High-throughput event processing on many threads without a queue between demultiplexing and processing, avoiding context switches, dynamic allocation, and data handoffs.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 2: Patterns for Concurrent and Networked Objects - Schmidt, Stal, Rohnert, Buschmann (2000)

elements.name: Lookup
elements.what: Resource providers register references with a lookup service under known names or properties; users query the service to find and access the resources.
elements.problem: Resource users should not hard-code the identity or location of providers; a mediating registry decouples acquisition from provider placement and lifetime.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 3: Patterns for Resource Management - Kircher, Jain (2004)
elements.borderline: Often distribution-flavored (naming services), but equally an in-process service registry; POSA3 documents it as a resource-acquisition design pattern.

elements.name: Lazy Acquisition
elements.what: Resource acquisition is deferred to the latest possible point - first actual use - typically behind a proxy that acquires transparently on demand.
elements.problem: Acquiring all resources up front wastes scarce resources and slows startup; acquire only what is actually used, when it is used.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 3: Patterns for Resource Management - Kircher, Jain (2004)

elements.name: Eager Acquisition
elements.what: Resources are acquired up front, before actual use (at startup or configuration time), and handed out from the pre-acquired set at run time.
elements.problem: Acquisition at use time is too slow or can fail unpredictably; paying the cost early makes run-time access fast and deterministic - central to real-time and embedded design.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 3: Patterns for Resource Management - Kircher, Jain (2004)

elements.name: Partial Acquisition
elements.what: A large resource is acquired in stages - only the part needed now, with further parts acquired progressively (e.g. lazy-loading pages of an image or file).
elements.problem: A resource may be too large or costly to acquire whole, yet partially usable; staged acquisition balances memory, latency, and availability.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 3: Patterns for Resource Management - Kircher, Jain (2004)

elements.name: Caching
elements.what: Released or fetched resources are kept in fast intermediate storage so re-acquisition is served from the cache instead of the expensive source, under an invalidation/consistency policy.
elements.problem: Repeatedly re-acquiring identical resources dominates cost; trading memory for re-use requires managing staleness, eviction, and consistency.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 3: Patterns for Resource Management - Kircher, Jain (2004)

elements.name: Pooling
elements.what: Released resources are recycled into a pool and handed out again on demand, amortizing acquisition/release cost across many uses; the pool manages size and eviction.
elements.problem: Frequent creation and destruction of expensive, identity-free resources (threads, connections, buffers, objects) wastes time and fragments memory.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 3: Patterns for Resource Management - Kircher, Jain (2004)

elements.name: Coordinator
elements.what: A coordinator drives a task spanning multiple participants through prepare and commit phases so either all participants complete their work or none do.
elements.problem: A task touching several resources/participants must not leave the system partially updated on failure; two-phase coordination yields all-or-nothing semantics at design level.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 3: Patterns for Resource Management - Kircher, Jain (2004)

elements.name: Resource Lifecycle Manager
elements.what: A dedicated manager component centrally controls the whole lifecycle of a class of resources - acquisition, coordination, optimization, and release - decoupling lifecycle from resource use.
elements.problem: When many users share many resources, per-user lifecycle handling causes leaks and conflicting policies; centralizing lifecycle management enables global optimization.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 3: Patterns for Resource Management - Kircher, Jain (2004)

elements.name: Leasing
elements.what: A resource is granted for a limited time; the holder must renew the lease to keep it, and expiry releases the resource automatically.
elements.problem: Resource holders that crash or forget to release cause leaks in loosely coupled systems; time-bounded grants make reclamation the default rather than the exception.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 3: Patterns for Resource Management - Kircher, Jain (2004)

elements.name: Evictor
elements.what: An evictor monitors resource usage and, under a configurable strategy (LRU, LFU, priorities), releases or swaps out the least valuable resources to bound consumption.
elements.problem: Long-running systems accumulate rarely used resources; systematic, policy-driven eviction prevents exhaustion while keeping hot resources available.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 3: Patterns for Resource Management - Kircher, Jain (2004)

elements.name: Explicit Interface
elements.what: A component's usage contract is captured in an interface type explicitly separated from any implementation class, so clients depend only on the declared interface.
elements.problem: Clients coupled to concrete classes inhibit substitution, testing, and evolution; reifying the interface as a first-class artifact decouples contract from realization.
elements.named_in: Explicit Interface and Object Manager: Two Patterns from a Pattern Language for Distributed Computing - Buschmann, Henney, Schmidt (EuroPLoP 2003)
elements.borderline: Close to the 'program to an interface' design principle, but published as a named pattern with concrete structure; included per over-inclusion rule.

elements.name: Introspective Interface
elements.what: A component offers a separate interface through which clients can query metadata about its capabilities, properties, and configuration at runtime.
elements.problem: Generic clients (tools, containers, scripting layers) must discover what a component can do without compile-time knowledge of its concrete type.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 4: A Pattern Language for Distributed Computing - Buschmann, Henney, Schmidt (2007)

elements.name: Combined Method
elements.what: Operations that clients commonly invoke as a sequence are combined into a single interface method executed as one unit (e.g. put-if-absent, open-and-read).
elements.problem: Call sequences across an interface boundary are non-atomic under concurrency and costly over process boundaries; combining them restores atomicity and cuts round trips.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 4: A Pattern Language for Distributed Computing - Buschmann, Henney, Schmidt (2007)

elements.name: Enumeration Method
elements.what: A collection owner exposes a method that applies a client-supplied operation to each element internally, instead of handing out an external iterator.
elements.problem: External iteration leaks collection structure and is unsafe under concurrent modification; internalizing the loop keeps traversal control, locking, and structure encapsulated.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 4: A Pattern Language for Distributed Computing - Buschmann, Henney, Schmidt (2007)

elements.name: Batch Method
elements.what: An interface method operates on a whole set of elements per call (bulk get/set) rather than requiring one call per element.
elements.problem: Element-at-a-time access across an expensive boundary (locks, IPC, network) multiplies overhead; batching amortizes the boundary cost over many elements.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 4: A Pattern Language for Distributed Computing - Buschmann, Henney, Schmidt (2007)

elements.name: Half-Object plus Protocol
elements.what: A logically single object is split into two coordinated half-objects, one per address space, each implementing the locally needed functionality, kept consistent by a private protocol between them.
elements.problem: An object is needed in two places at once (e.g. client and server) with low-latency local behavior on both sides; neither pure remote access nor full replication fits.
elements.named_in: Half-Object + Protocol - Gerard Meszaros, in Pattern Languages of Program Design (1995)
elements.borderline: Distribution-motivated, but the mechanism is a concrete object-splitting design implementable within one codebase; POSA4 documents it as a design pattern.

elements.name: Context Object
elements.what: Execution-scoped state (security principal, transaction, locale, request data) is bundled into one context object passed along the processing path instead of via globals or long parameter lists.
elements.problem: Components along a call chain need shared per-activity state without global variables, thread coupling, or interface pollution with pass-through parameters.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 4: A Pattern Language for Distributed Computing - Buschmann, Henney, Schmidt (2007)

elements.name: Copied Value
elements.what: Value-typed objects are passed and stored by copy, so each holder owns an independent instance and mutation cannot cause aliasing surprises.
elements.problem: Sharing mutable value-like objects by reference invites unintended interference between holders and races under concurrency; copying restores value semantics.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 4: A Pattern Language for Distributed Computing - Buschmann, Henney, Schmidt (2007)

elements.name: Immutable Value
elements.what: Value objects are made unmodifiable after construction, so they can be freely shared and aliased - including across threads - without copying or locking.
elements.problem: Shared mutable values require defensive copies or synchronization; immutability makes sharing safe by construction and simplifies reasoning about state.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 4: A Pattern Language for Distributed Computing - Buschmann, Henney, Schmidt (2007)

elements.name: Execute Around Method
elements.what: A method (or scoped object) performs guaranteed paired actions - acquire/release, open/close, begin/end - around a client-supplied block of code.
elements.problem: Clients forget or fail to perform the closing half of paired operations, especially on error paths; centralizing the pairing makes correct usage the only possible usage.
elements.named_in: Smalltalk Best Practice Patterns - Kent Beck (1997)

elements.name: Null Object
elements.what: A do-nothing implementation of an interface stands in for 'no object', so clients invoke it uniformly without null checks.
elements.problem: Scattered null/None checks clutter client code and invite omission errors; representing absence as a polymorphic object removes the special case.
elements.named_in: Null Object - Bobby Woolf, in Pattern Languages of Program Design 3 (1998)

elements.name: Object Manager
elements.what: A manager component separate from both clients and managed objects controls the objects' creation, access, and destruction, issuing references while owning the lifecycle.
elements.problem: When object lifetime is governed by application-wide concerns rather than any single client, per-client ownership fails; a dedicated manager centralizes lifecycle policy.
elements.named_in: Explicit Interface and Object Manager: Two Patterns from a Pattern Language for Distributed Computing - Buschmann, Henney, Schmidt (EuroPLoP 2003)

elements.name: Lifecycle Callback
elements.what: A framework or container invokes designated component methods at defined lifecycle transitions (initialize, activate, passivate, destroy), inverting control of lifecycle handling.
elements.problem: Components hosted by a runtime must react to lifecycle events they do not drive; standardized callbacks let the host manage many heterogeneous components uniformly.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 4: A Pattern Language for Distributed Computing - Buschmann, Henney, Schmidt (2007)

elements.name: Methods for States
elements.what: Modal behavior is realized by swapping function/method references (or delegates) as the mode changes, so dispatch selects the current mode's behavior without conditionals.
elements.problem: Mode-dependent behavior via if/switch on a state code is error-prone and non-extensible; binding behavior directly to the current state removes the dispatch logic.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 4: A Pattern Language for Distributed Computing - Buschmann, Henney, Schmidt (2007)

elements.name: Collections for States
elements.what: Objects are placed in per-state collections; an object's state is encoded by which collection currently holds it, and state transitions move it between collections.
elements.problem: When many objects cycle through the same modes and are processed per mode, storing state in each object forces scans; per-state collections make 'all objects in state X' direct.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 4: A Pattern Language for Distributed Computing - Buschmann, Henney, Schmidt (2007)

parked_architecture.name: Layers (POSA1)
parked_architecture.why: Whole-system structuring into abstraction levels - the canonical architectural pattern.

parked_architecture.name: Pipes and Filters (POSA1)
parked_architecture.why: Architectural style: dataflow topology of a whole processing system (the in-process pipeline mechanism is a separate, smaller element other scouts may carry).

parked_architecture.name: Blackboard (POSA1)
parked_architecture.why: Architectural style for whole problem-solving systems with cooperating knowledge sources.

parked_architecture.name: Broker (POSA1/POSA4)
parked_architecture.why: Distributed-system topology / middleware structure.

parked_architecture.name: Model-View-Controller (POSA1)
parked_architecture.why: Application-level structuring of interactive systems.

parked_architecture.name: Presentation-Abstraction-Control (POSA1)
parked_architecture.why: Hierarchy of cooperating agents structuring a whole interactive application.

parked_architecture.name: Microkernel (POSA1)
parked_architecture.why: Platform/product-line level system structure (minimal core plus extensions).

parked_architecture.name: Reflection (POSA1)
parked_architecture.why: Two-level meta/base architecture for self-modifying systems - system-level structure in POSA1's formulation.

parked_architecture.name: Domain Model (POSA4)
parked_architecture.why: Application-scale organization of business logic (Fowler PoEAA origin); statement about whole-app structure.

parked_architecture.name: Domain Object (POSA4)
parked_architecture.why: Component-partitioning construct for structuring applications around self-contained domain concepts.

parked_architecture.name: Shared Repository (POSA4)
parked_architecture.why: System integration style: components coordinate through a central data store.

parked_architecture.name: Message Channel (POSA4, from EIP)
parked_architecture.why: Inter-system messaging infrastructure role; middleware topology.

parked_architecture.name: Message Endpoint (POSA4, from EIP)
parked_architecture.why: Inter-system messaging infrastructure role.

parked_architecture.name: Message Translator (POSA4, from EIP)
parked_architecture.why: Inter-system integration role (format mediation between systems).

parked_architecture.name: Message Router (POSA4, from EIP)
parked_architecture.why: Inter-system routing topology element.

parked_architecture.name: Client Proxy (POSA4)
parked_architecture.why: Broker-decomposition middleware role for remote invocation infrastructure.

parked_architecture.name: Requestor (POSA4)
parked_architecture.why: Broker-decomposition middleware role (client-side invocation machinery).

parked_architecture.name: Invoker (POSA4)
parked_architecture.why: Broker-decomposition middleware role (server-side dispatch machinery).

parked_architecture.name: Client Request Handler (POSA4)
parked_architecture.why: Broker-decomposition middleware transport role.

parked_architecture.name: Server Request Handler (POSA4)
parked_architecture.why: Broker-decomposition middleware transport role.

parked_architecture.name: Replicated Component Group (POSA4)
parked_architecture.why: System-level replication structure for availability/scalability.

parked_architecture.name: Container (POSA4)
parked_architecture.why: Component-hosting execution infrastructure (EJB/CCM-style); system-level runtime structure.

parked_architecture.name: Activator (POSA4)
parked_architecture.why: On-demand activation of services/processes (inetd-style); deployment/system-level resource mechanism.

parked_architecture.name: Page Controller (POSA4, from PoEAA)
parked_architecture.why: Web-application structuring pattern; app-level control topology.

parked_architecture.name: Front Controller (POSA4, from PoEAA)
parked_architecture.why: Web-application structuring pattern; app-level control topology.

parked_architecture.name: Application Controller (POSA4, from PoEAA)
parked_architecture.why: App-level centralization of screen/action flow.

parked_architecture.name: Template View (POSA4, from PoEAA)
parked_architecture.why: Web presentation-layer structure; app-structure flavored - a Fowler-focused scout may reclaim it downward.

parked_architecture.name: Transform View (POSA4, from PoEAA)
parked_architecture.why: Web presentation-layer structure; app-structure flavored - a Fowler-focused scout may reclaim it downward.

parked_architecture.name: Firewall Proxy (POSA4)
parked_architecture.why: Network security topology element.

parked_architecture.name: Authorization (POSA4, from Yoder-Barcalow)
parked_architecture.why: Security-architecture pattern (policy enforcement structure across a system); Phase 3 / security territory.

excluded_notable.name: Encapsulated Implementation (POSA4)
excluded_notable.why: Restates the encapsulation/information-hiding principle rather than naming a distinct implementable mechanism.

excluded_notable.name: Automated Garbage Collection (POSA4)
excluded_notable.why: Language-runtime memory management facility - below the design band as normally consumed (platform feature, not a design element one implements).

excluded_notable.name: Objects for States (POSA4)
excluded_notable.why: Alias of GoF State pattern; folded - GoF State is the canonical entry (GoF scout territory).

excluded_notable.name: Dynamic Invocation Interface (POSA4)
excluded_notable.why: CORBA-style runtime-composed invocation API; middleware-internal vocabulary with little life outside ORBs - recorded, not cataloged.

excluded_notable.name: POSA5: On Patterns and Pattern Languages (2007)
excluded_notable.why: Meta-theory of patterns and pattern languages (pattern form, sequences, languages); catalogs no implementable elements - noted per charter, nothing extracted.

excluded_notable.name: Counting Handle / Resource Cache / Resource Pool / Task Coordinator / Virtual Proxy (POSA4 names)
excluded_notable.why: POSA4 renames of already-cataloged mechanisms; folded as aka into Counted Pointer, Caching, Pooling, Coordinator, and Proxy respectively.

notes: Coverage: POSA1 9 elements (8 design patterns + Counted Pointer idiom; 8 architectural patterns parked). POSA2 all 17 elements, catalog verified live against Schmidt's Vanderbilt POSA2 page (all four groups). POSA3 all 10 elements, verified live via Wiley/O'Reilly listings with page numbers. POSA4 full ToC verified live via Schmidt's POSA4-TOC.pdf: system-level entries parked (30 parked total, listed individually); genuinely in-process, not-in-POSA1-3 mechanisms cataloged (15). POSA5 noted, nothing cataloged. Deliberate delegations (named in POSA4 but canonical elsewhere - left to sibling scouts to avoid duplicate canonical entries, flagged here so the merger can verify coverage): GoF re-documented patterns (Composite, Iterator, Facade, Mediator, Command, Memento, Decorator, Template Method, Strategy, Chain of Responsibility, Interpreter, Visitor, Object Adapter, Bridge, Abstract Factory, Builder, Factory Method) -> GoF scout; Future and Guarded Suspension -> concurrency scout (Lea/JCiP canonical); Data Transfer Object, Business Delegate, Data Mapper, Row Data Gateway, Table Data Gateway, Active Record, Message -> Fowler/enterprise scout (PoEAA/Core J2EE canonical); Double Dispatch (Beck SBPP / GoF Visitor discussion) -> GoF/smalltalk scout. POSA1 spot-check caveat: no single live page listed POSA1's full ToC this session; Counted Pointer, Proxy, Publisher-Subscriber, Whole-Part, Master-Slave, Command Processor confirmed on live pages (olemiss POSA notes, Goodreads, POSA4 ToC); View Handler, Forwarder-Receiver, Client-Dispatcher-Server marked established from deep familiarity (names are certain). Kind-axis judgment calls: Thread-Specific Storage under execution-concurrency (could argue state-management); Monitor Object under synchronization-coordination though POSA2 files it under concurrency; Component Configurator under resource-management (component lifecycle); Wrapper Facade / Extension Interface under construction-api.
